title: Background Neuromodulation has emerged as an essential therapeutic strategy in the treatment of neurological and psychiatric disorders [ 1 – 3 ]. This non-pharmacological treatment strategy is specialized in clinical conditions where traditional pharmacological or behavior modifications have adverse reactions and limited effectiveness, such as in Alzheimer’s disease (AD), Parkinson’s disease (PD), epilepsy, and depression [ 4 – 6 ]. By targeting brain regions and neural circuits, neuromodulation provides the perspective to directly influence abnormal brain states, thereby improving cognitive, emotional, and motor phenotypes in damaged individuals [ 7 – 9 ]. Since the effectiveness of these interventions might rely on their capability to modulate the brain’s neuronal oscillations across different neuronal oscillations, comprehending the relationship between neuromodulation and oscillatory activity is critical for enhancing treatment outcomes. γ oscillations are progressively identified as vital in recognizing the neural basis underlying psychological and cognitive processes such as perception, attention, memory, and motor functions. These oscillations have the potential as neurobiological markers for early detection, identification, and intervention of various brain disorders, offering the understanding of the dysregulated neural dynamics underlying various clinical symptoms [ 10 – 13 ]. Alterations in γ oscillations are identified to be relevant to adaptions in cognitive processes, emotional regulation, and neural plasticity [ 14 – 18 ]. Imbalances between excitatory and inhibitory processes, as mirrored in raised γ oscillations in the visual cortex including GABAergic interneurons, underscore the relevance of γ rhythms in maintaining neuronal homeostasis [ 19 , 20 ]. Besides, γ oscillations are modulated by metabotropic glutamate receptors (mGluRs), which also contribute to cognitive functions such as perception and attention [ 21 – 24 ]. As BF GABAergic projection neurons, particularly those containing parvalbumin (PV), play a critical role in triggering cortical γ oscillations. Optogenetic stimulation of BF PV neurons in mice preferentially increases cortical γ band oscillations (GBO) by entraining cortical oscillators at a resonant frequency of approximately 40 Hz, while inhibition of these neurons reduces GBO power [ 25 ]. This mechanism is independent of cholinergic neurons and likely involves synchronization of cortical PV interneurons. These findings highlight BF PV neurons as a potential therapeutic target for disorders involving abnormal γ oscillations, such as schizophrenia [ 25 ]. Overall, γ oscillations have rich biological implications in coordinating complex brain functions, positioning them as promising targets for neuromodulation [ 26 – 29 ]. Notably, γ oscillations have been linked to a series of neurological disorders, such as neurodegenerative disorders like AD and PD [ 30 ]. From the micro-perspective, decreased γ oscillations affecting microglial features have been found to precede plaque development in AD [ 31 ]. γ oscillations, generated by striatal cholinergic interneurons, play a crucial role in influencing movement actions within cortical-striatal circuits [ 32 ]. γ oscillations of inhibitory nerve cells after stroke have been observed to undermine vascular and lead to behavioral disorder [ 33 ]. Besides, γ oscillations have been linked to sensory perception, working memory, and motor control functions in patients with PD, and enhancing the γ oscillations could increase the plasticity of the primary motor cortex in PD [ 34 , 35 ]. Overall, the relationship between disrupted γ activity and abnormal brain functions of neurological disorders has been identified by neural evidence from macro- and micro-perspectives, emphasizing the further need for precise treatment with γ oscillatory neuromodulation. Besides, disturbances in γ oscillations have been highly related to a wide variety of psychiatric symptoms, with the restoration of these oscillations emerging as a prospective healing approach [ 36 ]. Modified γ activity has been related to psychotic symptoms in drug-naive patients revealing relationships between γ oscillatory patterns and the remaining symptoms [ 37 – 40 ]. Decreased γ oscillations of the limbic cortex have been observed in mice presenting anxiety and anhedonia-like habits [ 36 , 41 ], implying the relevance of oscillatory disruptions in schizophrenia. Furthermore, γ oscillations could help discriminate different disease states in mental disorders, such as anxiety, depression, or suicide risk [ 42 – 44 ]. Emerging studies indicate that modulating γ activity might alleviate many psychiatric symptoms in both animal models and humans [ 45 – 47 ]. Notably, previous studies highlight the role of basal forebrain (BF) γ oscillations in modulating the default mode network (DMN), a brain network linked to internally focused cognition and dysregulated in brain functional disorders. BF γ oscillations are elevated during quiet wakefulness and suppressed during externally directed tasks, mirroring DMN activity patterns [ 48 , 49 ]. In rodents, BF γ coherence with the anterior cingulate cortex (ACC), a key DMN hub, suggests functional influence [ 48 ]. A study confirmed that BF drives DMN changes during rest-task transitions, while the mediodorsal thalamus engages during internally focused cognition [ 49 ]. These findings underscore BF γ modulation as a therapeutic target for DMN-related disorders like epilepsy and depression, offering mechanistic insights into psychiatric symptoms. Despite the growing understanding of γ oscillations in neurological and psychiatric disorders, there is a significant gap in research specifically addressing the role of γ neuromodulations as a treatment strategy. The present review aims to bridge the gap by systematically examining how γ oscillations affect neurological and psychiatric conditions and the potential benefits of γ neuromodulations for patients. By thoroughly assessing the existing literature on γ neuromodulations from clinical perspectives, and identifying their physiological mechanisms and intervention outcomes, this review seeks to enhance our understanding of γ neuromodulations as promising therapeutic strategies, ultimately improving the efficacy of treatments for neurological and psychiatric diseases.

extracted_data.document_summary: This comprehensive review systematically examines the therapeutic potential of gamma ("\u03b3") neuromodulation as a non-pharmacological strategy across a range of neurological and psychiatric disorders, including Alzheimer's Disease, Parkinson's Disease, epilepsy, Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder, schizophrenia, and depression. It investigates various neuromodulation techniques (such as rTMS, tACS, tDCS, neurofeedback, DBS, VNS, optogenetic stimulation, and rhythmic sensory stimulation) to regulate neuronal oscillations, particularly \u03b3 oscillations and cross-frequency coupling. The document highlights the role of \u03b3 neuromodulation in improving cognitive, emotional, and motor functions by addressing oscillatory imbalances, reducing pathology (e.g., amyloid-\"\u03b2" accumulation), improving seizure control, and sharpening executive functions, while also discussing the physiological mechanisms, intervention outcomes, and the need for further research into specific treatment strategies and precision medicine.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Various neuromodulation techniques are investigated, including gamma (\u03b3) neuromodulation, repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS), transcranial alternating current stimulation (tACS), transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS), neurofeedback (including EEG-neurofeedback and olfactory bulb-driven closed-loop neuromodulation), Deep Brain Stimulation (DBS - including responsive DBS and high-frequency DBS of the habenula, fornix, posterior cingulate cortex, subthalamic nucleus, and anterior nucleus of the thalamus), Vagus Nerve Stimulation (VNS), optogenetic neuromodulation, Rhythmic Sensory Stimulation (RSS), multisensory \u03b3 stimulation, \u03b3 Knife Surgery, \u03b3 Entrainment Using Sensory Stimulation (GENUS), and high-frequency modulation.
treatment_details.dose_specificity: This review synthesizes existing literature and, as such, generally lacks specific dose-response data from new interventions. However, various dose details are mentioned for different neuromodulation techniques. Optogenetic stimulation increased cortical \u03b3 band oscillations (GBO) by entraining at approximately 40 Hz, with inhibition reducing GBO power. Multisensory \u03b3 stimulation was applied at 40 Hz, and 40 Hz \u03b3 entrainment via sensory stimulation (light flicker or sound) reduced amyloid plaques and tau pathology. rTMS is described as enhancing high-frequency oscillations (\u03b3, \u03b2) and reducing low-frequency rhythms (\u03b1, \u03b8, \u03b4), with low-frequency rTMS for epilepsy showing uncertain effectiveness. tACS synchronizes neuronal oscillations, directly entraining \u03b3 oscillations through phase-locked sinusoidal currents, sometimes targeting frontal areas. tDCS delivers low-level electrical currents to adjust cortical excitability. Neurofeedback (including EEG-neurofeedback and multisensory stimulation with operant conditioning) allowed for self-modulation of \u03b3-band synchronization, achieving up to 71% accuracy in enhancing neural synchronization in preclinical AD and older adults, with success rates for \u03b3 modulation varying (approximately 75%). DBS was applied to the fornix for AD, the posterior cingulate cortex for PD, the subthalamic nucleus (STN) for \u03b3 activity modulation, the subgenual cingulate or ventral striatum, and bilaterally to the anterior nucleus of the thalamus (ANT) for epilepsy, which reduced seizures by 40.5% at 3 months and 75.0% at 5 years. VNS aimed at desynchronizing epileptiform activity in the \u03b3 band. \u03b3 neuromodulation involved a rapid transition from an over-activated Cross-frequency coupling (CFC) pattern to an inhibited-activated state during stimulation, which remained significantly weakened post-stimulation. High-frequency modulation and high-frequency DBS of the habenula were also mentioned. The document notes a significant gap in research addressing specific, detailed treatment strategies with \u03b3 neuromodulations.

measured_effect.direction_of_change: highly variable (increases, decreases, modulation, enhancement, reduction, entrainment, dysregulation)
measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Optogenetic stimulation increased cortical GBO by entraining at approximately 40 Hz, while inhibition reduced GBO power. Elevated during quiet wakefulness and suppressed during tasks in BF; raised in visual cortex. Decreased prior to plaque development in AD, and in limbic cortex in mice with anxiety/anhedonia. rTMS enhances high-frequency oscillations and reduces low-frequency ones. tACS modulates and directly entrains \u03b3 oscillations. Neurofeedback achieved 71-75% accuracy in enhancing \u03b3 synchronization. Reduced frontal \u03b3 power (Cohen\u2019s d = \u22120.39) in schizophrenia. DBS to fornix activated \u03b3 oscillations; to posterior cingulate cortex modulated hippocampal \u03b3 oscillations; led to sub-harmonic entrainment and \u03b3 power suppression linked to tremor reduction in PD. Associated with levodopa-induced dyskinesia in PD. VNS desynchronized epileptiform \u03b3 activity. \u03b3 neuromodulation transitioned over-activated CFC to an inhibited-activated state, significantly weakened post-stimulation. Auditory steady-state responses (ASSRs) showed consistent deficits in schizophrenia. Cortical \u03b3 oscillations were modulated to improve OCD and depressive symptoms, correlating with depression severity. 40 Hz \u03b3 entrainment reduced amyloid plaques and tau pathology in AD models. Non-phase-locked \u03b3 oscillations (50-70 Hz) were induced by emotional stimuli. Dysregulated \u03b3 synchrony in basal ganglia-cortical circuits is pathological in PD. Disrupted by E/I imbalance in epilepsy, contributing to hyperexcitability. Abnormal \u03b3 power affects emotional regulation in psychiatric disorders.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Crucial for recognizing the neural basis of psychological and cognitive processes (e.g., perception, attention, memory, motor functions), emotional regulation, and neural plasticity. It mediates network-level communication, functional architecture, and brain network synchronization, impacting cognitive control, emotional processing, stability, stress responses, and flexibility. Gamma oscillations regulate cognition and behavior, modulate arousal, and attentional processes, and maintain neuronal homeostasis and the brain's excitatory-inhibitory (E/I) balance. They are involved in maladaptive habit learning, regulating habits and goal-directed behavior, influencing movement actions, and modulating the default mode network (DMN). Specific roles include amyloid-\"\u03b2" clearance, neuroinflammation, promoting neuronal synchrony, and reflecting GABAergic transmission and cognitive processing.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Neurological and psychiatric disorders including Alzheimer's Disease (AD), Parkinson's Disease (PD), epilepsy, depression, schizophrenia, anxiety, anhedonia, OCD, and stroke. Contexts also include cognitive processes, emotional regulation, neural plasticity, imbalances between excitatory and inhibitory processes, quiet wakefulness, externally directed tasks, rest-task transitions, and DMN modulation. Interventions include various neuromodulation techniques such as optogenetic stimulation/inhibition of basal forebrain (BF) parvalbumin (PV) neurons, rTMS, tACS, tDCS, neurofeedback, DBS (to various brain regions including fornix, posterior cingulate cortex, STN, ANT, subgenual cingulate, ventral striatum, habenula), VNS, Rhythmic Sensory Stimulation (RSS), multisensory \u03b3 stimulation, \u03b3-neurofeedback training, \u03b3 Entrainment Using Sensory Stimulation (GENUS), auditory stimulation, olfactory bulb-driven closed-loop neuromodulation, phase-dependent neuromodulation, and closed-loop brain stimulation. These are applied in contexts of emotional stimuli processing, working memory tasks, and preclinical AD/older adults.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Serves as a neurobiological marker for early detection, identification, and intervention of various brain disorders, indicating dysregulated neural dynamics, and predicting treatment efficacy. Alterations are relevant to adaptions in cognitive processes, emotional regulation, and neural plasticity; raised oscillations indicate E/I imbalances; decreased oscillations precede plaque development in AD. Disruption can undermine vascular integrity leading to behavioral disorder after stroke. It is linked to sensory perception, working memory, and motor control functions in PD, with enhancement potentially increasing primary motor cortex plasticity and improving motor function. Disturbances are highly related to psychiatric symptoms; restoration is a prospective healing approach and can discriminate different disease states in mental disorders. Modulating \u03b3 activity might alleviate psychiatric symptoms, improve mood stabilization, impulse control, emotional stimuli processing, cognitive control, emotional resilience, emotional stability, and reduce stress and psychotic symptoms. BF \u03b3 modulation is a therapeutic target for DMN-related disorders like epilepsy and depression. \u03b3 neuromodulation enhances neural synchronization, improves cognitive and emotional functions, alleviates OCD symptoms, reduces obsessive-compulsive behaviors, and facilitates adaptive responses. It is associated with deficits in working memory and cognitive impairments in schizophrenia, where restoration/enhancement aims to address these issues. In AD, \u03b3 modulation improves cognitive and behavioral functions, reduces amyloid-\"\u03b2" accumulation, and brain volume loss, and potentially slows neurodegeneration. In epilepsy, it indicates disrupted cognitive functions (SWC), predicts favorable surgical outcomes (HFOs), facilitates targeted interventions for seizure onset zone (SOZ) localization, highlights neuromodulation potential, and improves seizure control. It reflects the brain's capability to maintain optimum E/I equilibrium, vital for neurological and psychiatric health, where imbalance contributes to cognitive deficiencies and psychological dysregulation.
